title: Academic CV for PhD Applications: Structure and an Example
seoTitle: Academic CV for PhD Applications: Structure and Examples
seoDescription: Build an academic CV for PhD applications with clear project entries, accurate publication labels and evidence of your own research contribution.
intro: An academic CV should help a reader find evidence of your preparation quickly. Prioritise education, relevant projects, research experience and skills you can demonstrate; label publications and work in progress accurately.
description:
Start with the evidence the programme needs

An early-career academic CV should make your qualifications, research preparation and relevant skills easy to find. Use the programme's template and length limit where one is provided. Otherwise, choose a clear structure that gives the most relevant evidence enough space without listing every activity you have completed.

Put your name and professional contact details at the top. Include working links where they help the reader inspect relevant work. Add an ORCID or research profile only if you have one; do not create the impression of a publication record through an empty profile. Provide personal details such as nationality only where requested or relevant to the application process.

Education and research experience

List qualifications with the institution, subject, dates and accurate status. If a degree is ongoing, state the expected completion date rather than presenting the award as complete. Report grades in the original system unless the application provides a conversion method. A self-calculated UK classification should not be presented as an official award.

For a relevant project, explain the question and your contribution. Identify the methods you actually used, a result or decision you can discuss, and any shareable output. If the work was collaborative, distinguish your role from the team's overall achievement. A smaller task described precisely is more credible than a broad claim of leading research you did not lead.

An illustrative project entry

"[Project title] — [institution], [dates]. Investigated [specific question] using [method]. My contribution included [actual implementation, experiment or analysis]. Compared [baseline or alternative] under [documented conditions]. Produced [report, code or presentation where shareable]. The main limitation was [limitation you identified]."

Replace every placeholder with a fact. Include a numerical result only when you have measured it and can explain the conditions. A simulation experiment should be labelled simulation. Planned hardware tests should remain planned. The entry is a structure for reporting your own work, not a fictional candidate's achievement to copy.

Choose sections that fit your record

SectionUseful informationA boundary to keep clear
Research and projectsQuestion, contribution, methods and evidenceYour work versus collaborators' work.
Publications and outputsAccurate title, authorship, venue and statusPublished versus accepted, submitted or in preparation.
EmploymentRelevant responsibilities and decisionsA routine duty versus an independent research result.
TeachingRole, audience and responsibilitiesFormal teaching versus informal assistance.
SkillsRelevant techniques you can discuss or demonstratePractical experience versus introductory exposure.
AwardsActual award, awarding body and dateReceived awards versus pending applications.

Omit empty sections unless a template asks for them. If you have no publications, use the space for projects and other preparation rather than inventing a manuscript. A technical report or dissertation can be listed accurately without implying peer review. Check confidentiality and permissions before sharing links or documents from employment.

Make the document easy to inspect

Use consistent dates, clear headings and readable typography. Keep formatting simple enough to survive a PDF export. Check that links work and that symbols, line breaks and page breaks have not hidden information. A compact document is useful only if it remains readable.

Tailor the order and detail to the application. A research project relevant to the advertised methods may deserve more space than an unrelated role. Keep the factual history accurate while changing emphasis. Do not delete a material qualification issue merely because it is difficult to explain; use the application's guidance for relevant context.

References and final checks

List referees only when the application or template asks for them, and obtain their agreement before supplying details. Follow the specified number and submission process. A name on the CV does not replace a reference submitted through the required system.

Read the final CV beside the form and statement. Qualification names, dates, grades and output statuses should agree. Ask whether every claim could be explained in an interview. Revise vague praise into a factual contribution, or remove it when it adds no evidence. Keep a copy of the submitted version so that later updates do not obscure what the programme received.

Audit each claim before sending the CV

Read every project bullet as though an interviewer asks what you personally did. Replace a team-level claim with your own contribution where necessary. If the project produced a result, describe it accurately and keep the conditions visible. A simulation result should not be presented as a hardware demonstration, and a classroom exercise should not be labelled an independent research appointment.

Publications need particularly careful status labels. Published, accepted, under review, submitted and in preparation are different categories. Use the category that is true at the time of submission. Do not add a journal name to an unsubmitted draft in a way that implies acceptance.

Check evidence and labels together

CV itemWhat the reader needs
Research projectQuestion, your contribution, methods and a result or limitation.
Technical skillA credible level of use, preferably supported by a project.
Collaborative workYour role separated from the group's overall output.
Publication or reportAccurate title, authorship and current status.
LinkA working destination containing material you have permission to share.

Use consistent dates and qualification names across the CV, forms and statement. If a document uses a local degree title, add a concise explanation where useful without inventing an official equivalence. Tailor the order of sections to the programme's needs while retaining an accurate history.

Is a two-page CV compulsory?

Follow the call's limit. A concise early-career CV can often fit within two pages, but the right length is the one that meets the instructions and presents relevant evidence clearly.

Use links as evidence, not decoration

Link to a project report, repository or presentation only when it helps explain a relevant contribution. Check that the destination opens without a private login if public access is intended, and identify any access restriction clearly. A broken or unexplained link can make useful work harder to assess. Keep confidential data and credentials out of shared material, and use a short description so the reader knows what the link contains before opening it.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • Oxford Careers: academic applications
